selfDescription: I like busy places when I know where I can take a break. I am good with instructions, but I also want people to ask what I would change about them.
openQuestions: How will she adapt when support is less familiar?
Will language study remain enjoyable when conversational demands increase?

name: Malik Harbin

background.family: Lives with his mother and stepfather, with regular weekends at his father's home; all three adults coordinate school and medical needs.
background.finances: Middle income; specialist care creates costs but essentials and activities remain stable.
background.geography: Pearland, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Black and white extended family, English-speaking, with contrasting preferences for very quiet and very crowded celebrations.
background.school: Public high school; juvenile idiopathic arthritis is supported with flexible seating, extra passing time, and remote participation during significant flares.
background.accessOpportunities: Community college events and Houston-area programs are available; he asks about seating, walking distances, and schedules before committing.

timeline.story: Malik liked running obstacle courses and arranging his mother's scarves into costumes. Adults remember him as a child who could turn a cardboard box into a stage within minutes.

He developed joint pain and was eventually diagnosed with juvenile arthritis. Treatment and physical therapy became familiar routines. He kept playing with friends, though he sometimes needed to stop earlier than everyone else.

A flare interrupted a soccer season. While resting, he began editing photos and designing outrageous haircuts on printed portraits. He returned to recreational kicking later but no longer wanted the team's schedule.

He helped a neighbor make posters for a yard sale and discovered that readable prices mattered more than dramatic fonts. Standing all morning was tiring, so he redesigned the table setup to work seated for part of the event.

An introductory coding class bored him until he could change a page's appearance. He enjoyed visual experimentation but found debugging tedious. At a family event he confidently introduced speakers while sitting on a high stool.

He began assisting with hair and costume preparation for school performances, using adapted grips on difficult days. He also liked chemistry lessons about mixtures, although his actual laboratory experience remained limited to ordinary school experiments.

Malik designs publicity for a student production and helps plan seating for audience members with access needs. His symptoms fluctuate. He wants opportunities that allow flexibility without assuming his interests must stay indoors or that every activity should be easy.

avoids: Debugging code without a visible goal
ambitions: Try an accessible summer workshop
He imagines an adult routine with interesting people, flexible hours, and energy left for spontaneous outings

selfDescription: Some days I can do a lot, and other days I need a different setup. I like making something look exciting, but I care whether people can actually use it too.
openQuestions: Which activities remain satisfying during symptom changes?
Does his interest in chemistry persist beyond visually striking experiments?

name: Mateo Rivas

background.family: Lives with his grandparents and mother; several relatives work in electrical trades, and family meals include lively technical arguments.
background.finances: Modest but steady income, with tools shared through relatives rather than purchased new.
background.geography: A small town north of Amarillo, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American and Salvadoran family connections; bilingual Spanish and English, with different expressions associated with different relatives.
background.school: Public high school with vocational courses and limited arts electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Amarillo College visits and regional youth programs are possible through school or family rides; advanced music instruction is mostly online.

timeline.story: Mateo sorted screws in his grandfather's workshop and made drumbeats with empty containers. He liked company while working but preferred that people not correct every small choice.
His grandmother let him prepare simple fillings for family dinners. He became absorbed in tasting small changes and was less interested in memorizing the formal names of ingredients.

He learned basic electrical safety from relatives and helped label disconnected parts. People began joking that his future was settled. He liked the equipment but also wanted to talk about a school poetry assignment no one remembered to ask about.

A visiting musician demonstrated digital sound mixing. Mateo spent months combining recorded kitchen noises into rhythms, learning through repeated attempts and short videos. His grandfather, initially skeptical, helped him build a stand for a borrowed microphone.

How will she manage cost estimates when stakes increase?

name: Jonas Loke

background.family: Lives with his parents and two sisters; an aunt and cousins in Beaumont host occasional visits and maintain frequent video calls.
background.finances: Modest stable income from a small delivery business and school cafeteria work.
background.geography: A small town outside Salem, Oregon.
background.cultureLanguages: Marshallese American family using Marshallese and English; household members differ in how much community activity they want each week.
background.school: Public high school with agricultural science, choir, and a regional vocational partnership.
background.accessOpportunities: Local community college events are easiest; Lamar-area public programs during Texas family visits are plausible, with nonresident costs and distance unresolved.

timeline.story: Jonas liked helping load empty boxes into the family van and asking which house came next. At home he planted seeds from fruit and was surprised that most did not sprout.
A school garden gave him a more reliable way to grow things. He enjoyed measuring leaves and disliked the competitive classroom chart that treated the tallest plant as the best.

He joined a children's choir and discovered he liked singing with others more than speaking alone. A cousin taught him simple video editing, but he preferred recording plant growth to making fast entertaining clips.

Jonas helped his parents plan a delivery route and enjoyed the practical geography. Customers' small talk felt awkward until he learned a few opening questions. He also began making tiny paper sculptures while listening to music.

A vocational workshop introduced welding, which relatives expected him to enjoy. He liked the precision but not the heat and protective clothing. He chose a horticulture elective afterward, without deciding whether that meant anything about future study.

He visited cousins in Beaumont and toured a community garden and public campus event. Humid-weather plants fascinated him. Back home he helped younger students compare growing conditions and learned to stop correcting every imperfect measurement immediately.

Jonas sings in choir, works in the school greenhouse, and occasionally rides delivery routes with a parent. He is considering a longer Texas visit but does not know whether the appeal is family, unfamiliar plants, or the idea of a different landscape.

avoids: Treating growth as a simple competition
motivations: Understanding why living things respond differently
Maintaining family connections without copying every family interest
ambitions: Compare the same plant in two climates
He imagines an adult home with room to grow plants and sing with other people, though he is unsure how far from family to live
struggles: Quiet participation can hide how much he knows

selfDescription: I do not mind repeating an observation if something living keeps changing. I like a group sound better than a solo, but I still want people to notice my part.
openQuestions: Would he enjoy horticultural work when it includes routine commercial demands?
What would a longer stay away reveal about his preferred distance from family?

name: Avery Farzan

background.family: Lives with their parents and a younger sister; relatives visit often, and the household makes room for both debate and silence.
background.finances: Middle income with consistent housing and a clear yearly activities budget.
background.geography: A small community outside Bryan, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Iranian American and Texan family; English and conversational Persian, with an interest in stories that change during translation.
background.school: Small charter school emphasizing science projects, presentations, and independent study blocks.
background.accessOpportunities: Blinn College and Texas A&M public events are within driving distance; peers often need to organize shared rides.

timeline.story: Avery enjoyed dressing family members for imaginary ceremonies and explaining the rules in long speeches. They also liked counting fence posts during drives, repeatedly losing the count and starting over without concern.

They began soccer and choir, preferring the quick shared decisions of soccer and the prepared structure of singing. At home they mixed harmless pretend cosmetics from colored water and advertised them with extravagant claims.

A class experiment showed that attractive colors could hide inconsistent mixtures. Avery liked the result enough to repeat it but disliked recording exact quantities. A teacher kept their enthusiastic explanation while asking for clearer evidence.

They wrote a story in two versions for relatives with different language preferences. The versions diverged, and Avery became interested in what translation changed. They also confidently volunteered to organize a class event and forgot several basic supplies.

Their charter school introduced longer independent blocks. Avery used some well and spent others polishing titles before beginning work. Soccer practice supplied useful external structure, while choir became less enjoyable under a director who changed plans abruptly.

Avery left choir but joined a community reading performance with a predictable rehearsal calendar. A science project about emulsions connected old cosmetic experiments with school concepts. Their partner kept the detailed log, revealing a skill gap Avery had mostly talked around.

They play recreational soccer, perform readings, and are trying to maintain their own experiment notebook. They are comfortable proposing ideas but less practiced in sustained measurement. Their vocabulary and confidence sometimes cause adults to assume more technical experience than they have.

avoids: Repetitive logging when its purpose is unclear
motivations: Connecting familiar experiences to new ideas
Being part of a lively collaborative group
ambitions: Complete a documented experiment independently
They imagine an adult life with friends close by, regular games, and enough variety that every week need not look identical
struggles: Presentation polish can replace basic work
practicalConstraints: Need external checkpoints for long projects

selfDescription: I can explain why an idea sounds interesting before I know how to carry it through. I am trying to make the notebook as real as the speech, without losing the part that made me curious.
openQuestions: Will better documentation reveal deeper enjoyment of experiments?
Which external structures support initiative without making activities feel controlled?

name: Elena Castillo-Brooks

background.family: Lives with her mother, stepfather, and baby brother; adults did not attend college and openly ask questions alongside her.
background.finances: Stable lower middle income from skilled trades and office reception, with careful saving for future education.
background.geography: Pasadena, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American and white family connections; English at home with Spanish used frequently among extended relatives.
background.school: Academically structured public charter with frequent tests, clear homework routines, and limited workshop space.
background.accessOpportunities: San Jacinto College visits, public libraries, and Houston-area museum programs are feasible through school trips or family weekends.

timeline.story: Elena liked memorizing songs and asking adults to quiz her about picture books. She avoided messy painting at first, then happily used a wide brush when nobody expected a recognizable picture.

She enjoyed school rules and quickly learned what counted as a finished assignment. At home she helped measure rice and water, finding satisfaction in a repeatable result rather than inventing new dishes.

Her grandmother began teaching her more Spanish through stories. Elena understood much more than she would say aloud, worried about errors. She also loved a museum's oversized building blocks but assumed real construction was something other people understood.

Good grades became a reliable part of her identity. A loosely defined art assignment upset her because she could not tell what the teacher wanted. Her mother helped her submit a choice she liked rather than repeatedly asking for the hidden correct answer.

She joined a book club and discovered that disagreement could improve discussion without anyone losing points. A chemistry unit appealed through its explanations, though she had little chance to design an experiment herself.

At a public workshop, Elena built a small wooden tray with guidance. She measured accurately, made one repairable mistake, and kept calling the result luck. Caring for her baby brother also showed her that instructions do not cover every situation.

She remains academically successful and is trying a weekend cooking group where participants adapt recipes. She wants more experience making and testing things, but unfamiliar tasks expose how little she trusts competence that cannot be confirmed by a grade.

demonstratedSkills: Responding patiently to a baby's changing needs
motivations: Learning beyond getting the expected answer
Making education understandable to her family
ambitions: Try another practical workshop and keep the imperfect result
She imagines an adult life with stability, close family contact, and confidence to attempt unfamiliar things without constant reassurance

selfDescription: I know how to be a good student, but I am still finding out how I learn when nobody gives me a model answer. The tray I made is on my desk, including the part I fixed.
openQuestions: How will she respond to sustained open-ended work with supportive feedback?
Will practical experience broaden or clarify her academic interests?

name: Micah Baptiste

background.family: Lives with his parents and older sister, with grandparents nearby; the family shares responsibilities and encourages interests beyond their small auto-parts business.
background.finances: Steady middle income with seasonal business pressures but no recent disruption to essentials.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American and Trinidadian family connections; English at home and conversational Spanish learned through school, neighbors, and customers.
background.school: Public high school with mock trial, robotics, choir, and ordinary laboratory science.
background.accessOpportunities: El Paso Community College events, UTEP outreach, libraries, and desert education programs are nearby; business shifts limit some weekends.

timeline.story: Micah liked making up trials in which stuffed animals argued about missing snacks. He was equally happy quietly arranging his sister's old costume jewelry into patterns, a habit adults rarely saw outside home.

He helped count inexpensive parts at the family shop and enjoyed asking what each item did. He disliked greasy equipment and learned that understanding a catalog did not require wanting to work on an engine.

A choir director noticed his sense of rhythm, and he liked the group sound. He also read mystery stories alone, often guessing an ending confidently and then defending the wrong guess long after new clues appeared.

He tried robotics with a friend and enjoyed building but lost patience with code. A teacher gave him a short public explanation to deliver; he sounded confident despite relying heavily on a teammate's understanding of the software.

Mock trial gave him enjoyable scripts and arguments. He began noticing that listening carefully could be more useful than speaking first. At the shop he learned to ask customers clarifying questions instead of guessing what they needed.

Micah left robotics for a season, then returned for a design challenge with more hands-on assembly. He made simple jewelry from discarded safe materials at home and showed it to friends only after they asked about a bracelet.

He balances mock trial, occasional choir projects, and shop shifts. A desert field outing has made him curious about outdoor science, though he has little camping experience. He is increasingly willing to say that an appealing possibility is something he has not actually tested.

avoids: Long coding tasks with no visible change
motivations: Understanding rather than merely sounding convincing
Keeping private creativity alongside public activity
ambitions: Try a supervised overnight outdoor program
He imagines an adult life with a close circle, a place for creative work, and occasional travel beyond familiar landscapes
struggles: Can defend first impressions too long
Assumes new activities will be easy before trying them
practicalConstraints: Heat limits timing of outdoor activities

selfDescription: I can sound certain while I am still figuring something out. I like talking things through, but some of my favorite work happens quietly at a table with tiny parts.
openQuestions: Will outdoor curiosity persist through heat, routine recording, and early starts?
How will he distinguish enjoyment of public argument from enjoyment of detailed inquiry?
